speechtext: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of and concurrence in amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 64, respecting dominion companies.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I move that these amendments be concurred in, and at the same time I wish to add that if after I have given an explanation hon. gentlemen wish to discuss these amendments in detail I shall ask leave to withdraw my motion and move the house into committee. The bill has been carefully considered by the select standing committee of the Senate on banking and commerce. For three days I attended the meetings of that committee. The changes which have been suggested do not change the purpose or intent of the provisions of the bill, but after careful consideration of the bill and of suggestions which were made to the committee by correspondence and otherwise certain valuable amendments have been proposed and unanimously adopted by the Senate. I would refer hon. members to item No. 21 appearing in the notice printed in the votes and proceedings of Friday, June 15, where the suggestion is made to strike out on page 36 line 32 of the bill, the words "knowingly and wilfully." That is an error either in printing or transcribing. The amendment made by the Senate was to strike out the two words "knowingly and." We had made a similar deletion in another section, and the Senate thought that this section ought to conform to our previous amendment.
The main amendment, however, appears at page 430 of the votes and proceedings. The bill prescribes heavy penalties, heavier than have heretofore been imposed in any companies act in Canada, and, after consideration of the whole bill, the Senate thought the bill should be amended to conform to the provisions of section 372 of the English Companies Act of 1929. For that reason they

Dominion Companies Act
proposed and adopted an amendment to this bill in conformity with and following verbatim this section 372 in the English Companies Act. The new section as amended will read as follows:
"207. (1) The persons to whom this section applies are directors of a company or corporation; managers of a company or corporation; officers of a company or corporation; persons employed by a company or corporation as auditors whether they are or are not officers of the company or corporation.
(2)	If in any proceeding for breach of or non-compliance with any of the provisions of this act or breach of or non-compliance with any of the provisions of the letters patent, supplementary letters patent, special act, or bylaws of a company or corporation, against a person to whom this section applies, it appears to the court hearing the case that that person is or may be liable in respect of such breach or non-compliance, but that he has acted honestly and reasonably, and that, having regard to all the circumstances of the case, including those connected' with his appointment, he ought fairly to be excused for such breach or non-compliance, that court may relieve him, either wholly or partly, from his liability on such terms as the court may think fit.
(3)	Where any person to whom this section applies has reason to apprehend that any claim will or might be made against him in respect of any such breach or non-compliance, he may apply to the court, as defined in paragraph (d) of section three of this act, of the province in which the head office or the principal place of business of the company or corporation is situate, for relief, and the court on such application shall have the same power to relieve him as under this section it would have had if it had been a court before which proceedings against that person for such breach or non-comnlianre had been brought.
(4)	Where any case to which subsection two of this section applies is being tried by a judge with a jury, the judge, after hearing the evidence, may, if he is satisfied that the defendant ought in pursuance of that subsection to be relieved either in whole or in part from the liability sought to be enforced against him, withdraw the case in whole or in part from the jury and forthwith direct judgment to be entered for the defendant on such terms as to costs or otherwise as the judge may think proper."
The commission which had under review the English Companies Act thought that in view of the heavy penalties there imposed a certain discretion should be given to the court trying an offence in respect of which these heavy penalties were imposed, so that if such alleged offender had acted honestly and reasonably and if having regard to all the circumstances of the case he ought fairly to be excused for such breach or non-compliance, the court may relieve him either wholly or partly from his liability on such terms as the court may think fit. The Senate were unanimous in support of that provision. Personally I think that under the circumstances it is just and should be accepted.
That is the only material change which, through Senate amendments, has been made to the bill. I move that the amendments be concurred in.
Would the minister indicate again the section from which the words "knowingly and" have been struck out?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, I would refer the hon. member to page 36, line 30 of the bill. The hon. member will recall that the committee of the whole in this House of Commons struck out those words in a similar section. Subsection 2 now reads:
If any director, manager, or other officer of the company knowingly and wilfully authorizes .. .
And so on. The words "knowingly and" were struck out because the word "wilfully" implies knowledge. The Senate thought this section should conform to the section with which we dealt previously.
The other section is No. 67, I believe?

speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, June 11, consideration in committee of Bill No. 92, to facilitate compromises and arrangements between farmers and their creditors-Mr. Bennett-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury) in the chair.
On section 2-Interpretation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, subsection 3 of section 2 stood. There was an amendment to add the words, "if so determined by the court," so that it would not follow as a matter of course that failure on the part of the farmer to carry out any of the terms of the proposal would be deemed to be an act of bankruptcy, but that it should be determined by the court. I think the amendment has been put through.

Will you please read the
amendment, Mr. Chairman?

The amendment was carried, as
I understand it, the other day. The amendment that has just been handed to me is the same. It is that subsection 3 of section 2 be amended by adding at the end thereof the words, "if so determined by the court."
Farmers-Creditors Act

I really feel that the section ought to be amended by striking out subsection 3. I do not know whether the Prime Minister would consider doing that, but I think that is really the way the section should be amended. If subsection 3 is to remain in the section, I doubt whether the amendment moved by the Prime Minister is definite enough. I do not think there is anything in the act to guide the judge as to the basis on which he shall make his decision as to whether the farmer shall come under Part I of the Bankruptcy Act if he fails to meet any of his liabilities. Once any farmer makes a proposal for the composition or arrangement of his debts he will very likely be compelled to go through with it, and if the arrangement that he suggests is not acceptable to any of his creditors any one of them can have the matter referred to the provincial board of review. On this board there is to be a judge, a representative of the debtors, and a representative of the creditors. There is no doubt at all as to the view which the representative of the creditors will take in almost every case. I think we can take it for granted that the representative of the creditors will naturally seek to have the farmer bound to pay under the arrangement the very maximum which he thinks it is possible to get. It is very difficult indeed to get a person to represent the debtor's viewpoint as faithfully as the representative of the creditors will represent their viewpoint. We know that from experience.
Why should that be so?

That has been our experience in the past. The debtor's representative looks at it more in a disinterested way. That has been our experience. I have seen men on the debt adjustment board who it seemed to me in some cases were inclined to favour the creditors' case more than the debtor's; at least they would lean that way. The judge, I think, in most cases is apt to adopt a legal or technical attitude and to be bound by the law. I do not think a judge's experience particularly fits him as a rule, for seeing all the difficulties from the debtor's' point of view. The debtor will not be present personally, I take it, before the board of review. Any such arrangement can be brought before the provincial board of review and once the board of review has given its decision the act says that there is to be no appeal from it, and the farmer is bound to sign any documents or papers which may be drawn up in connection with carrying out the arrangement which has been determined by the provincial board. That
[The Chairman.]
being the case I think we should be very careful to safeguard subsection 3. It reads now:
In any case where the affairs of a farmer have been arranged by a proposal approved by the court or confirmed by the board-[DOT]
That is the board of review:
-Part I of the Bankruptcy Act shall, notwithstanding section 7 thereof thereafter apply to such farmer and failure on the part of such farmer to carry out any of the terms of the proposal shall be deemed to be an act of bankruptcy.
The farmer for the rest of the time that he continues to farm, and it may be all his life, will be in a different position with regard to bankruptcy, from any man who has not had such an arrangement of his affairs. The very first year after the arrangement he might have a crop failure; there might be a drought, or the man might be sick and be unable to work his farm, and then immediately he comes under Part I of the Bankruptcy Act if so determined by the court. That is, his failure to carry out the terms of the agreement will be an act of bankruptcy, if so determined by the court. Even under the best of circumstances it seems to me that if this is to be determined by the court there should be some basis laid down to guide the court so that it would know on what principle to base its decision.
First of all I would like the Prime Minister to consider striking out subsection 3. I cannot see that striking it out would weaken the act in any way. I do not think it would affect the farmer's liability to pay his debts for he would be in the same position as any other farmer who could be compelled to pay his debts. But if there is a good reason for exempting farmers in general from Part I of the Bankruptcy Act, I do not think that failure to meet any of his obligations under this arrangement should immediately make that farmer subject to the terms of Part I of the Bankruptcy Act.
If the Prime Minister will not agree to striking out subsection 3 I suggest that he might enlarge the amendment he has proposed, to read something like this:
Provided that such failure was not caused by crop conditions or depressed prices or, without being restricted by the foregoing, by other causes over which the debtor had no control.
If those words were added to the subsection it would be a guarantee to the house that the farmer would not be forced under part 1 of the Bankruptcy Act through, as I have said, a crop failure, depressed prices or other conditions over which he had absolutely no control. If it is the purpose of this bill to

Farmers-Creditors Act
keep a farmer on his farm, I think we should either strike out this subsection or amend it as I have suggested. I should like to know if the Prime Minister would not consider changing subsection 3 in the manner I have suggested.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The basis of this legislation would be destroyed if that subsection were taken away. Section 7 of the Bankruptcy Act exempts a farmer from its provisions; this bill gives him the benefit of those provisions without assigning or without being adjudicated a bankrupt. Having secured an arrangement and an extension having been agreed upon or settled by the court of review, if there is nothing in the provisions to indicate that failure to observe the arrangement made shall constitute an act of bankruptcy, then the whole basis of the legislation disappears. You cannot have it both ways. You cannot have the benefit of the Bankruptcy Act under our jurisdiction to deal with property and civil rights without having a corresponding obligation that the failure to maintain the agreement arrived at shall constitute an act of bankruptcy. I was impressed with what was said the other day by the hon. gentleman opposite and to my right and realized that it was perfectly sound to provide that crop failures, climatic conditions and depressed prices should be factors to enter into the determination by someone as to whether the default is excusable or inexcusable. If excusable, then it does not constitute an act of bankruptcy; if inexcusable, it can be determined only by a judge in any event. I am sorry to say to the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) that that is as far as I can go and still maintain the jurisdiction of this parliament to deal with contracts, property and civil rights and questions of arrangements made between creditors and debtors.

I should like to know where there is anything in the bill to indicate to the judge whether he should determine that a man should come under Part I and whether his failure should be deemed an act of bankruptcy. We have the Prime Minister's (Mr. Bennett) statement, but as far as I can see there is nothing in the bill to indicate to the judge that that is the intention of parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not desire to prolong the discussion unduly but I endeavoured the other day to point out to the committee that Part I of the Bankruptcy Act deals with bankruptcy and receiving orders. Section 3 gives a long list of what constitutes acts of
bankruptcy. The judge, in determining whether or not he should adjudicate a defaulting party to this agreement as a bankrupt, would consider the whole condition of the applicant or the insolvent. The fact is that in every one of these cases that will have to be dealt with an act of bankruptcy has been committed, otherwise this would not apply. He is now getting away from the results of that act by availing himself of the provisions of this bill. If a judge so determines that he shall be given .a second chance, the inevitable result follows only when that determination has been made by a judge.

When a farmer makes a composition under this bill and endeavours to set himself up again to continue his life on the farm, he would probably apply to the farm loan board. I was wondering what would happen in those provinces where there is no farm loan board. Would a man in that case be able to come under the provisions of Bill No. 92?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He certainly would come under the provisions of Bill No. 92 but his ability to secure money would depend upon the provincial body which was functioning instead of the dominion body in that particular province. That would be a matter between the farmer and the provincial body because the farm loan board would not be transacting business in that particular province. Judging by what has been said in some communities, it is not improbable that he would be able to secure more generous terms from the provincial body than he would from the dominion board, although I am not expressing an opinion in that connection.

I should like the Prime Minister to make something a little more plain to me. I should like to know what will be the effect of the amendment and how the section will read when the amendment is incorporated.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This bill is based
upon the assumption that without assigning or being adjudicated a bankrupt a farmer unable to pay his debts may avail himself of what I would call the general provisions of bankruptcy, that is, arrive at an arrangement with his creditors by which they would not be able to proceed against him during the life time of the agreement or while its provisions were being met. On the other hand, he will be enabled to keep himself free, shall I say, from suit by having execution issued against him or anything of
Farmers-Creditors Act

that sort. The act as it reads provides that in the event of his failure to discharge his obligations under the compromise agreement, by reason of that fact he would be a bankrupt and the provisions of Part I of the Bankruptcy Act would apply to him, even though he were a farmer. Objection was taken to that the other day and it was pointed out that great hardship might be worked in the event of climatic conditions preventing a farmer from reaping a harvest or depressed prices preventing him from making a profit. I suggested that we add to the subsection such words as would prevent him from being ipso facto a bankrupt. He could be adjudged a bankrupt for failure to discharge his obligations under the compromise agreement only if the court so determined. In other words, default on his part to carry out the compromise agreement should not in itself render him a bankrupt; a judge would have so to determine before he would be a bankrupt in law and in fact. Having endeavoured to enable the farmer to secure the benefits of the Bankruptcy Act by interfering through legislation with contractual obligations, with property and civil rights, the basis of this legislation is that it shall not be a permanent incentive to him to escape the discharge of the obligation which he has thus undertaken, but rather that his ability to do so shall constitute an act of bankruptcy. Have I made myself clear?
Yes, thank you.

I do not think that the amendment which is suggested accomplishes the purpose which the Prime Minister has in mind. The section states that if a man has entered into an arrangement with his creditors and has undertaken certain obligations as part of that arrangement, he will then be subject to Part I of the Bankruptcy Act. It is not his failure which subjects him to Part I of the Bankruptcy Act but the fact that he has made a proposal. It then goes on to state that the failure of the debtor to carry out the proposal shall be deemed an act of bankruptcy. The Prime Minister suggests adding the words, "when so determined by the court." Now I submit that those words do not add anything at all to the section, because Part I provides for acts of bankruptcy being taken into consideration by the court, and you always have to have the court determine whether an act of bankruptcy has been committed. I think therefore that the section as it reads now, and even with the Prime Minister's amendment, will mean that a man who has entered into a proposal and undertaken certain obligations becomes 
liable under Part I of the Bankruptcy Act, and that provides that certain things are acts of bankruptcy and involve the determination of the quality of those acts by the court itself. So I submit that adding the words "when so determined by the court" does not get us further along the road which the Prime Minister desires to travel.
The other point I want to make is this. I doubt whether after all this is beneficial to the persons for whose benefit the act is being passed, even if the Prime Minister went further and made it clear in his amendment that the failure of the debtor to carry out one of the terms of the proposal should not be deemed an act of bankruptcy unless the court, in the exercise of special discretion, so decided. It seems to me that the insertion of words making it clear that the failure to carry out the proposal is not necessarily an act of bankruptcy will make creditors that much more reluctant to afford credit to the farmer. They will say, "What happens is this. We give credit to the farmer. We know there is an act in force which permits of compromise but we know further that even after he has agreed to the terms, or after the board of review has ordered that it shall be effective, the farmer has no incentive to carry it out, because even if he does not carry it out his failure may not be deemed an act of bankruptcy." I question therefore whether, in the interests of the class whom we are trying to benefit, the insertion of some clause negativing the idea that failure to carry out the obligation is an act of bankruptcy will be useful and beneficial to those for whom its remedial provisions are intended.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
My thought was that clause 2, subclause 3 was put there for the purpose not of getting jurisdiction over the subject matter but of providing some sort of incentive to the farmer who had once made a compromise indicating to him he could not do this again and that after he had made his compromise he had to live up to it or be subject to the provisions of the bankruptcy act.
Farmers-Creditors Act

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is partly true.

That is why it seems to me, if that was the only purpose of subclause 3, it goes further than the Prime Minister intended. The clause brings the farmer under the Bankruptcy Act for the purpose not only of defining what shall be an act of bankruptcy but of giving a creditor the right to apply for a receiving order in view of the fact the farmer has not paid his bills, one of them being the undertaking he has entered into under the proposal. I thought the jurisdiction was covered by clause 6 which says that a farmer who is unable to meet his liabilities as they become due may do so and so. That, it seems to me, was the well known definition and test whether a man was bankrupt:	If you found a man in that condition,
parliament had jurisdiction by reason of the fact he was not able to meet his liabilities as they became due.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But the Bankruptcy Act does not apply to him-my hon. friend has put his finger on the point-until the compromise arrangement is completed and approved either by the court or the board. That is the whole point.
L understood clause 6 was the operative clause which provided that a farmer who was not able to meet his liabilities as they become due might make a proposal for a composition-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
-that the Bankruptcy Act does apply-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

only to such a man and that the act was made applicable by reason of clause 6. Subclause 3 of clause 2 was inserted, as I thought, for a totally different purpose. That is why I pointed out that that subclause had gone much further than the Prime Minister intended and that was the reason he was putting the rider on so that it would read:
Failure on the part of such farmer to carry out any of the terms of the proposal shall he deemed to be an act of bankruptcy-
And then the addition:
-if so determined by the court.
I still think the addition of those words does not affect the purpose which the Prime Minister has in mind because it seems to me Part I of the act cannot apply unless there is a determination by the court; that is to say, the act of bankruptcy is proved to the court

and the court decides whether it is an act of bankruptcy. The subclause says that failure on the part of the farmer to carry out any of the terms of the proposal shall be deemed to be an act of bankruptcy, with the addition by the Prime Minister of the words "if so determined by the court," but I think he would have to go further and say that notwithstanding there was failure on the part of tihe farmer it should not be deemed an act of bankruptcy unless the court, taking into consideration all the facts and circumstances and working on an entirely different principle from that on which a judge in bankruptcy generally works, decided it was an act of bankruptcy.

In the event of the secured creditors being willing to give an extension of time to the debtor can any non-secured creditors press the farmer into a position he does not want to attain, for instance, into bankruptcy? In other words, can a non-secured creditor press a farmer into bankruptcy even though the secured creditors are willing to negotiate with him?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid I have failed to make myself clear to this committee.
Well, the matter is pretty complicated to a layman.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I agree with that. If the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth is unable to follow me I would not expect a layman to do so, and I attribute the failure to myself and not to others.
Quite so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
First may I point out that the foundation of this whole matter lies in the	fact that by common law	there	canbe no	compromise by a	debtor	with	his
creditors unless all his creditors are agreed.
Mr.	MOTHERWELL:	Secured	and	unsecured?Mr.	BENNETT: Yes,	secured	and	unsecured. I should like to make that proposition so clear to the committee there can be no doubt about it; in other words, if ninety-nine per cent of a debtor's creditors agree to a compromise, that does not effect a compromise and the remaining one per cent may bring an action, secure judgment and issue execution. That is point number one. Number two is that under the law as it now stands farmers are not under section 7 subject to Part I of the Bankruptcy Act. Number three is that this bill endeavours to meet the situation without putting the farmer into bankruptcy in the first instance and uses the machinery
Farmers-Creditors Act
and power of parliament under its exclusive jurisdiction over bankruptcy to assist in making effective a compromise in which all the creditors do not join and need not join because of the character of the proceeding. The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth. is quite right in saying that clause 6 says what might be done; that is, when the farmer is not in a position to pay his debts and desires to make a compromise, his creditors are convened and they put forward a scheme of settlement or compromise.
Without bankruptcy.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, that is the point I am trying to make. That compromise would under the common law have no value in the world as being effective among the creditors and clause 2 is the one where we have to provide the jurisdiction required. Even at the risk of wearying the committee I should like to read this. Clause 2, subclause 2 reads:
Unless it is otherwise provided or the context otherwise requires, expressions contained in this act shall have the same meaning as in the Bankruptcy Act, and this act shall be read and construed as one with the Bankruptcy Act, but shall have full force and effect notwithstanding anything contained in the Bankruptcy Act, and the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act and bankruptcy rules shall, except as in this act otherwise provided, apply mutatis mutandis in the case of proceedings hereunder including meetings of creditors.
I can quite understand the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth assuming that subclause 3 was being used for the purpose he suggests, but I want him to study it for a moment. It reads:
In any case where the affairs of a farmer have been arranged-
That is the operative word there.
*-by a proposal approved by the court or confirmed by the board as hereinafter provided-
It is quite clear that unless we bring that within the Bankruptcy Act, the common law prevails and the compromise has no value.
I go back to clause 6.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
But clause 6 has no
reference to the Bankruptcy Act; it only enables the conference to take place.

It has reference to the
state of bankruptcy.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, what by law is one of the states of bankruptcy. After the proposal has been made and approved by the court or board, we have to have something to give authority and power to that settlement to make it legal as against the common law that there can be no compromise. There-74726-256
fore we say that the provisions of Part I apply and section 7 is no longer operative. The farmer's failure to discharge his obligations under that compromise agreement might continue for a very long time; it might continue without any action being taken, but the suggestion was made the other day of safeguarding this in some way and so we say that that shall not constitute an act of bankruptcy unless so determined by the court.

Supposing a farmer has obligations to meet and he can meet them only in part; can the mortgagee or the people to whom he owes money apply under this measure to the board of review in order to bring about a compromise or composition, and if they can apply, after that application is made and the composition is brought about, does that man, although not desirous of being a bankrupt, automatically become one unless the court takes all the circumstances into review?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: But under this act he is the only one who can make application?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Circumstances may arise, as we will see in the bill, in connection with difficulties and differences arising in which a creditor can make a further application, but not the original application.

Then may I ask the Prime Minister this question. Under certain circumstances, as I understand the bill, the people to whom the farmer owes money can make an application, and the composition is arrived at?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

His creditors cannot
apply under the act?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The jurisdiction rests
with the farmer and not with the creditors.
The farmer has to make the first move under this bill?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I think it is quite clear that the farmer makes the first move under this bill, but after the farmer makes his proposal

Farmers-Creditors Act

eventually the provincial board has power to make an arrangement and the farmer has no option but to accept it. He must sign any papers he is ordered to sign.
Then he becomes bankrupt.

No, he does not, but he places himself in the position that if he fails to meet any of the payments which he is obliged to make, that shall be deemed an act of bankruptcy under Part I of the act. That brings me to the statement made by the Prime Minister. I think he made it very clear that the reason for putting in the words he suggested was that if the failure to meet the payments as arranged was due to crop failure or climatic conditions, then the farmer should not be considered a bankrupt, because those were conditions over which he had no control.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He might not be considered a bankrupt; the court would have jurisdiction.

Those are the reasons the court would take into consideration for refusing to have him deemed a bankrupt. But if that is the reason for inserting these words I really think some suggestion to the judge should be included as well, as to why he should not determine the man to be a bankrupt. There is nothing in the act to guide the judge in refusing to give an order directing that the man is a bankrupt, and I think the amendment I have suggested should be inserted for that purpose. My amendment is that after section 3 we add the words, "provided that such failure was not caused by crop conditions or depressed prices or, without being restricted by the foregoing, by other causes over which the debtor had no control." As I understand it that would leave it to the judge in rendering a decision to say, "Parliament wishes me to be guided by the conditions laid down in the statute. Has the failure of the farmer to meet his obligations arisen through crop conditions or from other causes over which he could have absolutely no control?" In that way I think we would lay down a basis on which the judge could render a decision. It seems to me there is nothing in the act at present to suggest to the judge that if crop conditions were bad he should refuse to adjudge the man a bankrupt.
As I understand the act, and I should be glad if the Prime Minister would correct me if I am wrong, once a proposal is made the provincial board may make the final arrangement. It may be quite different from the

proposal of the farmer in the first instance, but on the application of any creditor the provincial board can review the case and decide on the terms of the compromise, and the farmer must accept those terms. Of course the creditors must accept them too, but in making these adjustments no leeway seems to be left to the farmer; it is not anticipated that he will have any equity other than what he is going to pay for under the compromise. It seems to me that unless the farmer has more protection than he is given here he may say, "I might far better remain as I am and still enjoy the privilege of living in my own home, because my only reason for making this compromise would be to try to assure to myself the privilege of living here."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: His exemption is not taken from him by bankruptcy.

No, and his exemption cannot be taken from him by a court of law, but I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether this legislation in any way invalidates the debt adjustment legislation in the provinces.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, it would not be competent for us to validate or invalidate it. May I repeat, even at the risk of being tiresome, that legislation enacted by a legislature somehow must fall within the provisions of section 92 of the British North America Act, and be exclusively within the jurisdiction of that legislature. Legislation passed by this parliament somehow must fall within the provisions of section 91, either under the specific heads enumerated or the broad general terms of peace, order and good government in Canada. If we passed an act to attempt to validate what has been done by a province it would be a contradiction in terms, for if the exclusive jurisdiction rests with the province and exclusive jurisdiction rests with parliament-there are two or three matters in which there is concurrent jurisdiction, with which I need not deal-it would follow that an attempt under our exclusive power to validate something that exclusively belonged to a province would be a contradiction in terms.
Has the board of review power to lower the interest rate on a mortgage or other debt that now exists, which the farmer must pay for the years covered by the new agreement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I should say the answer would be no; that is dealt with by section 17. My hon. friend is talking about future interest?

Farmers-Creditors Act

Yes. The farmer now has a mortgage bearing interest at eight per cent, we will say. Under this compromise the principal of that mortgage may be reduced, but would the board have power to say that the rate of interest should be five iper cent or six per cent or any rate other than that set out in the existing mortgage?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: After the decision of the supreme court the other day it is not contemplated, except to the extent mentioned here, that they may deal with secured and unsecured creditors as well. It does not contemplate the board having power to break a contract, with the exception of the provision under section 17 dealing with the question of interest.

That would only apply
to secured creditors or those having security; it would not necessarily apply to unsecured creditors, who might get any rate of interest or no interest whatever, as the board might decide.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Offhand one would say,
considering the kind of cases that will have to be dealt with, that here the whole arrangement is predicated on the ability of the man to pay. There need be no plan at all. If the board concludes that the man will never pay they should not make an arrangement. This is predicated on the assumption that the man has indicated, by his past history or by his present surroundings and conditions, his ability to pay something. He makes a compromise accordingly, and from what was said the other day by the representatives of the secured creditors, I feel quite certain that in their anxiety to keep the man upon the security, upon the land, they will be most generous in their attitude towards interest rates. Many of them, as I explained to the committee the other day, have already reduced their interest rates, indicating their earnest desire to keep the farmers on the land. I suppose no one wants to keep the man on the land any more than the people who loaned the money to him; surely that would be the case. They are the people who want him to stay there. He wants to stay there, for one reason, to have a home, to make his living and to pay his debts. And they want him to stay there in order that their security may not become useless.
I say to the hon. member for Macleod that we have not undertaken, and I hope parliament will never undertake, to do what is regarded to be of the utmost danger. I will put it this way, that there are those who would say that it would be invalid for us to 74720-256 i
do it. I tried to explain that, ordinarily, parliament has jurisdiction over interest, but once a contract is made between a farmer and a loan company, or an insurance company, or his neighbour to pay a given rate of interest, that contract is then solely under the exclusive jurisdiction of the province, being a matter of property and civil rights. There are those who say notwithstanding that fact we have a right to say that although one of the terms of the contract is that he shall pay seven per cent we may say that hereafter he will pay only three per cent. But I think legal opinion is that it is not competent for us, that it is no longer a matter of interest, but that it is a matter of a contract between one citizen and another citizen or-if you wish to accept my illustration-between a citizen and a company. And there is no jurisdiction on the part of this parliament then, to interfere with such contract. We think that we have gone as far as we can in section 17. In fact, I do not know whether or not some of my legal friends think that section 17 is wholly within our powers; I think it probably is. We have gone as far as we think we can, to be certain. To suggest that this parliament can pass a statute and say that a contract between Smith and Jones by which Smith agrees to pay Jones five per cent can be changed to an agreement to pay one per cent, in the view of legal men with whom I have discussed the matter is to suggest something that is not within our power: I do not know the view held by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth but I may say that is the general view among legal friends with whom I have discussed the matter. It would be within the power of the province to do it, and, of course, it would amount to confiscation. The privy council has decided in the Florence Mining case that that is a matter within the competence of a provincial legislature. In that case the mine was taken from one person and given to another, and they were denied the privilege of going to court and issuing a statement of claim. It was held by the privy council that that was a constitutional and valid exercise of the powers of a provincial legislature. My view is that it is not competent for this parliament to interfere with property and civil rights, after a contract has been arrived at.
Do you consider section 17 is within our power?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I say section 17 is, we think, within our power. We believe it is. I think section 17 is valid, because it refers only to interest and to matters arising solely out of it.
Farmers-Creditors Act
My right hon. friend must think it is valid or he would not have it in the measure.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There are doubts. We think it is.
It may be what may be termed a line question.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I may have misunderstood
the Prime Minister, but I thought he said that this parliament had no power to change a contract. From his remarks I drew the inference that we had no power to reduce mortgage interest from eight per cent to live per cent. But I understood it was intended that under this legislation, the provincial board would have power to render a decision in regard to the composition of a farmer's debt, and one of the things it was expected they should do was to write down the capital debt, even in the case of secured creditors. I wish to have that point cleared up.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member did
not misunderstand me. We have provided in section 3, the one with which we are now dealing, that under certain circumstances the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act shall apply. Last session we enacted some legislation by which we did provide for adjustments with respect to secured creditors. It was contended by very able members of the legal profession that that was beyond our competence. The supreme court unanimously decided that that was within our jurisdiction. I do not know whether the case is to be taken farther or not, but as the law now stands these provisions are predicated upon that decision. As the law now stands we have framed these provisions, and they were framed so as not to be considered in this house until after judgment was given. If the judgment had been adverse I am afraid I should have had to modify them. They do, in terms apply to secured and unsecured creditors, and if the hon. gentleman has before him the statute passed at last session he will see how far we really did go.

If I am correctly informed,
in almost all cases where reorganization might be effected under the legislation passed last year the interest on bonds and other securities would be reduced, and it seems to me they are being reduced under the authority of the legislation passed last year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But they are not compulsorily being reduced. That is what I have been trying to say to the hon. gentleman.

The bankruptcy court has
power to reduce. Not being a lawyer I may be labouring under considerable difficulties. But I should like to be clear in the matter. If we have power to legislate giving the bankruptcy court or any bankruptcy machinery the right to reduce the principal of a debt, surely we have the power to give them the right to reduce the rate of interest which is to be paid by a debtor under a new arrangement. I just wish to find out whether the provincial boards, when they made those final settlements between debtors and creditors which are binding upon all parties, have any authority or power in law to fix a lower rate of interest, which the farmer is assuming under the compromise, than was said to be payable by him under the original contract.

There is only one
point with which I should like to deal. I am sure the Prime Minister will understand our position. As he said, this matter is somewhat involved. Many of us are in the unfortunate position of being laymen, and yet we will be called upon to explain all the minute details of this legislation to those people in our constituencies who may be interested. It is for that reason, among others, that we are endeavouring to ascertain an exact understanding of the legislation.
As I understand it, with respect to the provincial legislation a farmer will have the choice between remaining under the present provision for provincial debt adjustments and coming under the provision of this new federal legislation. He cannot have both. In other words, if he elects to enter into composition under the provisions of the federal legislation he thereby loses any opportunity he may have had to continue under the provincial legislation. I believe that point may have been in the mind of one of my colleagues when he suggested that this legislation would invalidate the provincial legislation. I cannot see that it would do that, but I believe it would give an alternative to the farmer. He could come in under either the provincial or the federal, but he could not come under both. Once he has come under the federal legislation he has placed himself under the terms of federal bankruptcy law, which would override any provincial legislation.
The one point, however, in which I am keenly interested, and which has been discussed at great length, is the question of protection afforded to a debtor after a composition has been entered into and after, for reasons under or beyond his control, he has failed to comply in full with those conditions.

Farmers-Creditors Act
The Prime Minister, realizing the situation, introduced an amendment to-day so far as possible to cover the point. But the difficulty
1	have in my mind is this: As I understand it the amendment-and I agree with the hon. member for Shelburne-Yanmouth, although it may be presumption on the part of a layman to state whether or not he agrees or disagrees -but so far as I understand the Bankruptcy Act such protection is provided under that act, itself. This goes a little farther than does the act. What I have in mind is this. It is possible, if not probable, that any court before which such a case might be brought might conceive itself bound by the statutory definitions of what constitutes insolvency, and might therefore merely determine whether or not in view of those statutory definitions the debtor was insolvent and therefore subject to Part I of the Bankruptcy Act. I was wondering whether it would be possible to enlarge the section somewhat along this line, that in its determination the court should not be bound by the statutory definitions of insolvency but should have full discretion in dealing with the matter. Otherwise it does seem to me-I speak subject to correction- that the average court would feel itself bound in such a case by the statutory definitions laid down in the Bankruptcy Act itself. That act defines what bankruptcy and insolvency is, and I think that the average judge will feel that he has no choice in the matter except to decide whether the farmer was actually insolvent according to the act itself.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon.
gentleman from Red Deer has put the case very clearly from his angle. I can only say to him that if he will look again at subsection 3 of this bill, and then at section 7 of the Bankruptcy Act, and then at section 2 of the Bankruptcy Act, he will have these matters before him. Section 7 says that a farmer shall not be subject to the Bankruptcy Act. Section 2 defines what are acts of bankruptcy. Now this statute says that in the event of a farmer failing to discharge the obligations which he has undertaken, section 7 of the Bankruptcy Act shall no longer apply to him, and failure on the part of the farmer to carry out any of the terms of the proposal shall be deemed to be an act of bankruptcy. There has to be failure to carry out any of the terms of the proposal. It has nothing to do with section 1 or section 2 or anything else. It makes it referable only to this one single thing. He cannot be made a bankrupt under section
2	because that is precluded by section 7, but section 7 does not apply when there is
failure on the part of the farmer to carry out any of the terms of the proposal. That is what we say in this bill, that failure to carry out any of the terms of this proposal shall be deemed to be an act of bankruptcy if so determined by the court.
My hon. friend from Macleod suggests that we add words to the effect that it shall not be deemed an act of bankruptcy if the farmer's failure to carry out the terms of the proposal should be caused by climatic or economic conditions. Now we have a rule of law, whether it is sound or not, and I suppose laymen will doubt its soundness, that when you mention specific things you thereby exclude the others, and it was because of that I thought it desirable to leave the matter so wide and so clear that when a judge looks at, say, the six terms in the proposal -one relating to production, for example, one with relation to cultivation, one relating to residence, one to the taking of moneys that come from the sale of the crop for tax purposes, and so on-that a breach of any one of these terms shall be deemed to be an act of bankruptcy; if so determined by the court. That is an entirely different thing from the Bankruptcy Act. It is an application of it. Under this statute we say, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Shel-burne-Yarmouth, that when the proposal has been approved by the court the operative provisions of the Bankruptcy Act apply when there has been default, shall I say, in any one of the terms of the agreement. Instead of trying to anticipate what the terms would be and what default would be we simply say "if so determined by the court." If there are other words that make the farmer's position safer I am most anxious to adopt them, but I must keep in mind that if I undertake to specify certain things I have excluded those I do not mention, and we may run up against that difficulty in the very first case, whereas, as it stands now, it applies to every possible contingency that can arise in connection with default in relation to any of the terms of the agreement. If there are wider words to be used to indicate a greater discretion, I am content to use them, but frankly I do not know what they are.

That was the only
point in my mind, that the farmer would be subject to Part I of the Bankruptcy Act as soon as the proposal was made, and if he failed to comply with the terms of the agreement the Bankruptcy Act would apply and he would be subject to its terms. Apparently I have not been able to make myself clear, but the one point I had in mind was this:
Farmers-Creditors Act

If the farmer breaks one of the terms of the agreement would the board have any discretion in applying to that case, say, the ordinary rules of insolvency and bankruptcy? Would they be able to say:	This man is
insolvent because of something beyond his control, and therefore the act does not apply to him, and therefore he should not be deemed insolvent? My impression is that as it stands they would not be able to say that, but would simply ask themselves:	Is
the farmer insolvent under any of the definitions in the Bankruptcy Act itself? If so, he must be declared a bankrupt and a receivership may be applied for.
My hope was that it might be made quite clear-frankly as a layman I would hardly care to suggest the words to be used-that the judge would be unhampered in his discretion and beyond applying the statutory definition of insolvency he would be able to take into account all these mitigating features and be able to say: There has been a crop failure and therefoi'e we shall not declare you an insolvent, and you will not be open to a receivership. My only desire is to make certain that absolute discretion is given to the court in such cases so that no judge would feel himself bound by the strict letter of the Bankruptcy Act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Bankruptcy Act does not apply to this section.
I understood the Prime Minister to say that just as soon as the farmer made the proposal he lost his immunity under Part I of the Bankruptcy Act.
As soon as the proposal is confirmed.

Yes, as soon as it is confirmed by the court and accepted by all parties the farmer loses his present immunity under Part I of the Bankruptcy Act and is then like any other citizen, but he could not be declared a bankrupt until he failed in the performance of one of the terms of the agreement; but having so failed, then under the amendment which has been moved by the Prime Minister it remains for the court to determine whether the man shall be declared a bankrupt in the ordinary sense of the word and be subject to a receivership.
My point was, and it is so essentially important that I repeat it, that it should be made quite clear in the act that after all the preliminaries have been gone through and the man has failed in one of the terms of the agreement, the court in making its determination shall be able to take into account
IMr. Speakman.]
the mitigating circumstances-hail, for instance, depressed prices, climatic conditions- but without indicating these conditions in the bill, and indicating only that the discretion of the court is absolute in such matters.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I suppose lawyers have differed, hence they have lived.
That is why we go to the privy council.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
"VVe will see that this does not get that far. Subsection 2 provides that the Bankruptcy Act applies mutatis mutandis but that where there is any conflict between the Bankruptcy Act and this statute, this statute shall prevail. That is, this statute shall supersede the Bankruptcy Act. Section 3 of the Bankruptcy Act has no reference at all to this legislation. If I were asked to name the points upon which I would regard a farmer bankrupt, and if it were desired to do it without any regard to this statute, I would do it under (f), which states that a debtor commits an act of bankruptcy when he ceases to meet his liabilities generally when they become due. In this case his liabilities are specifically indicated in the agreement which he has undertaken and, therefore, he comes within this. However, the point which I have apparently not succeeded in making clear to the committee is this: To found jurisdiction is one thing, to exercise it is another. To found it we must do it on some basis of fact, not of law, and that basis of fact must be that the farmer himself has applied to his creditors to adjust and compromise his obligations. That is a condition precedent to everything; that starts the thing. I think we are all agreed about that. When, having done that, he is able to make an arrangement and ultimately it is settled by the board of review, the provisions of the Bankruptcy Acit apply as provided by section 2, that is, the extent to which they are not at variance with this statute. Where they are at variance, this statute prevails. Subsection 3 reads:
In any case where the affairs of a farmer have been arranged by a proposal approved by the court or confirmed by the board as
hereinafter provided, part I of the Bankruptcy Act shall notwithstanding section 7 thereof thereafter apply to such farmer and failure on the part of such farmer to carry out any of the terms of the proposal shall be deemed to be an act of bankruptcy.
The hon. member's remarks have brought about some doubt as to whether or not that is abundantly clear, although in my mind it is clear enough that the only act of bankruptcy would be the failure to carry out the compromise provided by this bill. That is the whole genius of this legislation. Subsection (f) of section 3 states that the failure to pay liabilities generally as they become due constitutes an act of bankruptcy while this legislation deals with the agreement or proposal. The whole purpose was to make it clear that that was the only provision which would apply, namely, the provision regarding failure on the part of the farmer to observe the terms of his agreement and which, under the general provisions of section 3, would constitute an act of bankruptcy. If subsection 2 is applied to the whole statute I think it will be found that the court would construe those words to mean that an act of bankruptcy must be an act which arises out of the failure to comply with the terms of the agreement. If there is any doubt as to that. I should like to have it made abundantly clear.
Do not the first five words of subsection 3 really mean that the farmer would immediately come under the Bankruptcy Act?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, but the Bankruptcy Act is amended by this bill and this bill has supremacy over the main act. Subsection 2 deals with that and I ask my hon. friend to look at it. Instead of reenacting the whole thing, we take advantage of the Bankruptcy Act but with respect to this particular thing, we deal with it specifically. I think we can meet the last point raised by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) and the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote). I think that would

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I mentioned them.

subsection 3, which states that the failure of a farmer to carry out the terms of a proposal shall be deemed to be an act of bankruptcy, these words should be added, "provided that such failure was not caused by crop conditions or depressed prices and, without being restricted by the foregoing, by other causes over which the debtor has no control." haps this would circumscribe the authority of the judge but so far as I am concerned, I would prefer to have these words in. Provided that such failure shall not be deemed an act of bankruptcy unless in the opinion of the court such act was not due to causes over which such farmer had no control.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Or "causes beyond the

Yes. Then it might

There is another point on which I should like a little information. I understand that a farmer who is insolvent will not come under the provisions of this bill. This morning I handed the Prime Minister a letter I received from a farmer who declared that he was hopelessly insolvent, and who wanted to know if this bill would give him any assistance. To-day a farmer who is insolvent requires from $100 to $150 to go into bankruptcy. Many farmers simply cannot raise that money, and I was wondering whether under the provisions of this bill, by which we are providing without cost official receivers and boards of review for the benefit of those farmers who may come under the act, these insolvent farmers might not have their cases reviewed so that, if they are found to be hopelessly insolvent, they might be put through bankruptcy without the cost that is now entailed. These men cannot raise the money necessary to go through bankruptcy and they find themselves chained, as it were, almost as slaves. They are unable to get rid of this debt and start up afresh. I am sure that if some means could be provided whereby they could be relieved of this burden many of them would make a fresh start with at least some hope of making a livelihood.
I want to congratulate the Prime Minister on bringing in this legislation. I think it is very badly needed and will afford a great deal of relief to those who are able to come under the provisions of the bill. But I think hon. members, especially those from western Canada, will agree that many farmers in the west are hopelessly insolvent, and they will not geit relief so long as they remain in that condition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

The reason I answered the hon. gentleman as I did with respect to the case which he suggested might come within the provisions of the statute was that I had regard to subsection (9) of section 12, which reads:

Farmers-Creditors Act
course I have already indicated. I do not see that anything further can be done for bona fide farmers than is being done under this act.
I wondered whether, through the officials set up under this bill, such farmers could not go through bankruptcy without a charge of 8150, which it is impossible for them to raise.

Unless he applies for it?

a bankrupt.

quite clear, but I do not see how it would come under this act which is to keep farmers on the land rather than to help them off it. Did I understand the Prime Minister to say that under the terms of the Bankruptcy Act at the present time a farmer could not make a voluntary assignment?

A voluntary assignment

As a matter of fact the

Am I to understand that legal machinery is provided by which the farmer may take advantage of this act? Are there any provisions in the act giving the farmer legal aid without expense to him, in order that he may secure the benefits afforded under this act? For instance, we have provided counsel for returned soldiers applying for pension; is something like that being done under this act? speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I made it very clear-the hon. member could not have been in the chamber-that this act was framed in very simple terms. All a farmer has to do is indicate that he is unable to meet his obligations; then the official receiver who is appointed for each constituency takes up the matter and the costs incidental to it are charged against the consolidated revenue fund. The farmer escapes any costs.
Farmers-Creditors Act
Did the Prime Minister look into the question as to whether or not those people under the farm loan board or soldier settlement board could take advantage of this legislation.?

speechtext: I am not clear as to whether they could or not, without divesting the crown of some of its present authority under the act. speechtext: Well, that brings the crown into the position of dealing with a question of compromises, having already remitted S85,000.000 in connection with these matters. But I do not think that at the moment it is desirable. I am not sure, but that is my present view.

May I refer to a matter which was mentioned by the hon. member for Selkirk? I believe there really is some necessity in certain cases to have counsel for the farmers, if we expect any great number of them to take advantage of the legislation. It is true that the farmer may make his own proposals for the composition of his debt, but it is also true that any one of his creditors may appeal to the provincial board. The board then has power to review the whole case and to fix the terms of the composition or arrangement. As I said before, the farmer must accept that arrangement. On the board of review there will be a representative of the creditors. We can take it for granted that the creditors will see that they have high priced and very capable men to look after their interests. But I do not see how we can ensure that there will be representatives for the debtors who will take the same intelligent interest in their cases. Such a person could not be as well posted in the cases of individual farmers. The representative of the creditor would be well advised because in every case the creditor concerned would take the trouble to see that counsel was well advised and that his case was well presented. But I am afraid that the representatives of the debtors will not be in that fortunate position, even if they wanted to do the very best they could for the debtors.
A remedy for this condition may appear to the Prime Minister to be somewhat difficult, and he may think we are asking too much. I believe however that in many cases

the debtor will be in the hands of counsel, just as applicants for pension are in the hands of counsel when they come before the pensions board. I should be very glad indeed if the Prime Minister would give some consideration to the proposal to make it possible for the farmer to have the advantage of counsel.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My own view is that the farmer would be infinitely better if he presented his own case before a tribunal than he would be with the aid of counsel. He will make the statement of what he has got, what he can do, and demonstrate his capabilities and capacity to meet the situation which has arisen. If he cannot get more sympathy from a court than he can get from a lawyer, I greatly mistake his position.

It would be all right if the farmer could appear before the board of review, in the event of that board travelling around as does the pensions board. In that way the farmer could appear before the board and state his own case.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We contemplate that.

I did not understand that that would be done. I do not suppose that the board of review will see the farmer or hear his own side of the case. It would have nothing but the farmer's statement, and the case presented by the representative of the debtor who, perhaps, might act in a hundred cases. He would represent the cases of hundreds of debtors, and I do not think he would be able to look after the debtors' interests as well as the representative of the creditors would look after the creditors' interests. Unless the judge happened to be a man inclined to take the human view of a case I am afraid that the decisions, in the great majority of cases, would be inclined to favour the creditor rather than the debtor.

The house resumed from Monday, June 11, consideration in committee of Bill No. 93, to amend the Canadian Farm Loan Act- Mr. Bennett-Mr. Fraser (Cariboo) in the chair.
