subtopic: PROVISION TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I have a suggestion to make
to the Prime Minister. Those who are under this act will not be able to take advantage of Bill No. 92 which we have just passed, according to the interpretation that was given by the Prime Minister, and I think some consideration should be given to those who are carrying the load under the farm loan act, and if at all possible the interest rate should be reduced. We have a federal post office savings bank in this country paying 24 and 3 per cent interest, and I do not see why that money could not be loaned to the farm loan board, the two interest charges amounting to 4| or 5 per cent. No farmer can afford to pay 6 per cent. I make that suggestion on behalf of those who are carrying the load and who do not come under the bill we have just passed. This bill gives to the farm loan board further security but very little help to those who are burdened with loans they have obtained under this act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
All I can say is that you
cannot get money to lend on farm loans in this country at 24 or 3 per cent. The farm loan act provides that the moneys loaned should be loaned at 14 per cent more than is paid for the money. If the money is borrowed at 3 per cent the farm loan board lends it at 44 per cent. The farm loan board is not the government by any means, nor is the government the farm loan board. The farm loan board exercises an independent jurisdiction and makes its loans without reference to the government or anybody else, but the government has so far bought about ten million dollars of securities issued by the farm loan board to put it in funds to make the loans. The provision here is to enable an increase in the sum to be loaned in order that we may take care of those who have no capital, and we are dealing with that in section 9, making it a little more specific than it now is about supplementary advances.
I can only say that it would be quite impossible to take the money out of the post office savings banks and lend it on farm loans. If we did we would have a situation in this country that other countries have
405S
Farm Loan Act

had, namely, frozen, assets with which to meet the demands of depositors for their money. As it now stands, we have to maintain ten per cent in gold, metallic coverage, for post office savings, and that has been the law in this country for a very long time in order that post office savings may always be available to depositors who desire to get them. Depositors have to give so many days' notice of their intention to withdraw.

subtopic: PROVISION TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: In connection with this bill and the bill we have just been considering I am afraid there is not very much relief being afforded to the farmers of Prince Edward Island because the farm loan act has never been made operative in our province. Many of our farmers would like to obtain some new money at a lower rate of interest, but I think in this bill or in the other bill it is provided that a farmer can obtain immediate assistance in the way of an additional loan through this act only if he is paying an interest rate of over seven per cent. Is not that correct?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: That is not it. Section 17 of the act we have just passed is what the hon. gentleman had in mind.

subtopic: PROVISION TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Down in Prince Edward Island seven per cent is the highest rate of interest that is charged on any mortgages out at the present time, and possibly a lot of mortgages are out at six per cent, so the provision in this act whereby only those who are paying an interest rate of over seven per cent can avail themselves immediately of its provisions would not be of very much help to our farmers even if the act were brought into effect in our province.
There is another point. It is really too bad that this legislation cannot be made effective in all the provinces. I do not suppose parliament can force any province to adopt the legislation, but an effort should be made to ;reat every province alike, and every inducement should be held out to the local governments to embrace this legislation. If anything could be done to induce the province of Prince Edward Island and others who are not under the scheme to come in, it would possibly help out if, as I have said, the rate of interest mentioned in the bill were changed to suit maritime conditions.

subtopic: PROVISION TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I think the time is coming when drastic action will have to be taken to bring about a lower rate of interest, because agriculture cannot continue to carry on at the present rate of interest or even at six per cent. I had a letter this morning pro-[Mr. Bennett.1
testing against this legislation if the interest rate is going to be on a six per cent basis. They are now paying six per cent to the farm loan board, and there is an amortization clause whereby they pay an extra two per cent, so that if a farmer is to keep up his contract he has to pay eight per cent. I think everyone is agreed that eight per cent cannot be paid, especially under the conditions that have existed for the last few years. If the farmer gets behind in one of his payments, he is charged eight per cent on the overdue account. Bill No. 92 which we have just passed will no doubt bring a great deal of relief by the composition of debts, but in my opinion, if it is to be a success, the farmer must be in a position to meet the new arrangement, and his ability to do that will depend largely on the rate of interest he has to pay.
I might add that a more sympathetic attitude on the part of the farm loan board, especially provincial boards, is very much needed. I confine my remarks in that respect entirely to the provincial boards because I have always received very courteous treatment from the commissioner and the officials in Ottawa, but I cannot say the same of the provincial boards. There is a great deal of dissatisfaction with their administration.
Twenty years ago the United States sent a commission to Europe to study rural credits. Mr. Harvie Jordan, who was one of the commissioners, after a study of the situation, said:
Every European country for the past half century had given every possible assistance to the development of agriculture.
He found that in Europe farmers secured loans at four per cent while commercial loans ran from five to six per cent. That is just the reverse of the practice in this country and the United States, where commercial loans are made at cheaper rates than agricultural loans. In 1894 France passed the first fundamental law creating machinery for agricultural credits. Two years later, when the charter of the Bank of France expired, it was renewed only on condition that the bank advance to the government forty million francs free of interest to be used in subsidizing rural credit banks. It also stipulated that the bank should pay annually a sum calculated at one-eighth of its circulation, said sum to be not less than two million francs, for the same purpose. We are extending the charters of our banks for another ten years and I was wondering whether a clause of that kind should not be inserted. It was stated also by Mr. Harvie Jordan that loans to agricultural cooperative societies in Europe were made at rates as low as two per cent. As I stated before, the

Farm Loan Act
farmer in Canada cannot continue to pay the high rates of interest which are being charged.
While I am on my feet I Bhould like to refer to the complaints being made with regard to the administration of the Canadian Farm Loan Act. We are amending this act and I think we have some right to say under what regulations or under what conditions the provincial boards shall carry on. Farmers complain that they do not even get copies of their mortgages. As the Prime Minister knows, very often payments in western Canada are made by the delivery of grain. In the last few years when a farmer got behind the board demanded that he should sign a contract to deliver one-third or some other fraction of his crop. There is a great deal of dissatisfaction in connection with this delivery of grain as to wl at authority the board has to hold or sell the grain. I know of one case in Septemiber, 1931, where the board seized three hundred acres of crop for the payment of $294. When the crop was threshed the farmer had 4,300 bushels of wheat and 3,300 bushels of oats besides his green feed, and yet the whole crop was tied up from September to November. Through his solicitor the farmer delivered 1,000 bushels to the sheriff on November 14. At the price of grain prevailing on the day the tickets were delivered, this represented sufficient to cover his payments. Instead of selling this grain, the board held it and acknowledged receipt on December 4, two weeks later, when there had been a further drop in the price of grain. In January they wrote to the farmer to find out what he wished done wtih the grain and he wrote back stating that he expected to get the price prevailing on the day the grain was delivered. The grain was held for eight and one-half months during which time the price continued to drop. It was finally sold by the board at a considerable loss to the farmers. I took up this case and after a great deal of negotiation an adjustment was recently made of approximately $100. I am doubtful whether this man is going to be satisfied as there was a period of two weeks during which a considerable drop occurred in the price of grain.
I have another case where a farmer delivered grain in April of this year on the understanding that if, when it was sold, it did not bring in enough, he would pay the difference. The board wrote back saying that they would not accept any responsibility for the sale of this grain. He wrote back and said that that was quite satisfactory, that he wished to sell it himself. However, when
the rise in prices occurred about two weeks ago the board sold the grain, but it still did not bring sufficient to pay the farmers' debt.
I believe the price to-day is higher than when it was sold, even allowing for the recent drop in prices.
When the board accepts grain I think there should be some definite understanding with the farmer as to how and when it is to be sold. This would eliminate a great deal of controversy and misunderstanding. I understood the Prime Minister to say a while ago that he had no responsibility for the provincial boards, but this act has been created by this parliament. I understand that we are going to guarantee these bonds and surely we should have some right to say how the act shall be administered by the provincial boards.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
There is nothing that
can be added to what has been said so frequently during the last few weeks regarding interest rates. An earnest effort has been made to reduce interest rates in this country by inducing the banks to pay a lesser rate on deposits, but there has been considerable difficulty because of the fact that trust and loan companies under provincial charters are receiving deposits and paying an interest rate in excess of that paid by the chartered banks. This difficulty has been overcome to some extent, but it still prevails.
The hon. member has pointed out that in the conception of the Canadian Farm Loan Act it was assumed that much of the administrative powers would be left with the provincial bodies. Each province has its own registration laws and particular regulations touching the registration of documents, how mortgages are to be created and concerning the signatures of a man and his wife, and matters of that sort. Some have the old fashioned idea of a mortgage under which the fee or title to the property is transferred to the mortgagee with the right of redemption. Others go under the Torrens system whereby a mortgage constitutes a charge against the property. All these matters were in the mind of this parliament when it enacted the farm loan act, so that cooperation between the provincial and federal authorities is essential to its success. In a broad and general way I think it may be said that they have worked fairly well, although there are exceptions. I know of many cases myself to which objection could be taken, but when the explanations were received they do not appear to be nearly as bad. Acting in my own personal capacity and not in any official capacity, I have complained several times
Farm Loan Act

with respect to what I conceived to be the attitude taken by some of the provincial boards. After the depression some of them apparently became very fearful in connection with their record of the amount of loans and were unduly apprehensive as to collections and perhaps pressed their debtors very hard, in my judgment too hard. I gave the figures the other day which were supplied by the commissioners as to the amount of principal and interest in arrears, and judging from the observations made, most hon. members of the committee thought it was a rather large sum.
In connection with the taking of grain for the purpose of meeting obligations, I need hardly point out that two great cases in this country deal with the obligations of those who take securities. One noted case that went from the Yukon to the privy council against one of our banks dealt with the question of sale of securities at a low market, and there is a much more recent case. The board is no more immune than any other lender from the rule that it must exercise reasonable care and diligence in the marketing of wheat which it receives, and if it failed to do so it would be liable. But that would be in the absence of agreement. There is always difficulty. Of course, whenever it happens that a man's grain is sold on a rising market and it goes higher a few days later, he is perfectly satisfied that his creditor should have held the grain until it had reached the highest price. But if it falls then he is equally censorious of the creditor for not having sold it when it reached the high point from which it departed on the day he complains. These are but manifestations of human nature to which we are all subject, and most of us have been through the unpleasant experience of seeing our securities sometimes sold for less than we thought they were worth to pay our debts. Sometimes we have had to do it ourselves and sometimes others have done it for us. I can Dnly say that the rule is quite as applicable to the board as to any other lender who takes a security to protect himself against loss and under proper circumstances there is no doubt that the appropriate remedy against the board would be in the hands of the debtor.

speechtext: My point was that the board should have some clear understanding with the farmer, when they accept the grain, whether the wheat should be held, whether they should use their judgment, or just exactly what would be done. In one case they held it and in another case they sold it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

If the market suddenly goes down there is complaint because he should have sold when it was at the top point. I agree that there should be a hard and fast arrangement between the mortgagor and the board, when grain is taken; there should be a direction to sell at a fixed price which is the subject matter of agreement. I shall speak to the commissioner, directing his attention to what has been said to-day in that regard.

I have the act from the library but I have not had time to go through it. I have not found it in the marginal notes. If it is in the act I should like the Prime Minister, before passing the bill out of committee, to consider the advisability of changing that section, because I think that 1J per cent under certain circumstances is too high. The differential which the board must receive depends very largely on the amount of business it is carrying on. If the board were lending a larger amount of money, one per cent ought to be ample. I should like to see this change made in the act, either reducing the rate to one per cent or leaving it in the hands of the governor in council to fix from time to time.
The importance of reducing interest rates on farm mortgages is difficult to exaggerate. The loan value of any land under this act is going to be determined by its productive capacity; in other words, on the prospective net earnings of the farmer. It is going to depend on the value of the commodities which can be produced on the farm, less actual and necessary costs. That is to say, it is the farmer's margin over his costs, and the rate of interest in reality fixes the loan value of the property. Let me make that clear.
Let us say that the margin which the farmer has is estimated at $120, and suppose he has a loan of $2,000 drawing interest at the rate of eight per cent. The interest is $160, so that

Farm Loan Act
no additional loan is possible, under this act, to that fanner. At seven per cent the interest would be $140 and no new loan is possible. If it were six per cent the interest would be $120 and still no new loan would be possible. At a rate of five per cent the annual charge would be $100 and there would be a surplus available to pay interest on a larger loan. In other words, it would increase the loan value of the farmer's property to the extent of $400. So that with a net income of $120, at five per cent, the loan value of the property is $2,400; at six per cent the loan value is reduced to $2,000; at seven per cent the loan value is $1,700, and at eight per cent, $1,500. The rate of interest payable on the farm mortgage might in reality be said to fix the loan value of the property, and I think I am right in saying that a reduction in the rate of interest is the most important factor in working out this whole scheme. For that purpose I am now discussing the two acts together, the farm loan board act and the measure now before us.
I urged in the house before, when this legislation was being considered, that action should be taken by law to reduce the rate of interest on farm mortgages to a certain specified rate. Personally, I should be in favour of five per cent. I believe the Prime Minister said that there was represented in' farm mortgages the sum of $726,000,000. I think we are safe in estimating that of that amount $300,000,000 is at eight per cent and perhaps $300,000,000 at seven per cent. If you reduced the rate of interest to six per cent, that would effect a reduction in interest charges of $9,000,000 annually, and at five per cent the total interest burden would be reduced $15,000,000. If the rate were fixed at five per cent the reduction which would be effected in the annual interest charge on farm mortgages would amount to a total of $15,000,000. I mention this to show that I am not overemphasizing the importance of this matter, and it is involved in section 5 of the bill, which deals with the amount that may be loaned on mortgage.
The value for loaning purposes is going to be fixed very largely by the rate of interest which is payable on farm mortgages. I am not unmindful of what the Prime Minister said before. He intimated that he had given consideration to this suggestion, but one reason why he could not see his way clear to take the action proposed to reduce the rate of interest was that some companies had issued debentures some of which were payable in the old country at a rate of five per cent, and that obviously these companies could not continue 74726-257
to pay five per cent on such debentures if they themselves were allowed to collect only five per cent. I suggest that he could deal with that situation by amending the farm loan board act in such a way that these companies could come to the board with debentures bearing four per cent and get the money neeessary to pay off the debentures which they owe in the old country.

As I have said in the house before, it is not the size of the debt that matters so much as the rate of interest which the debt carries. As a farmer I can pay five per cent on a mortgage of $8,000 more easily than I can pay eight per cent on a loan of $5,000. There are in Canada thousands of farmers paying eight per cent on mortgages, and so far as I can see, this legislation is not going to bring them any relief to many of them. interest rates. I did intend to argue under clause 17 of the other bill that perhaps a clause might be inserted in that bill to reduce by law the rate of interest on mortgages. Some people may say that that is unfair, but we are dealing with actual conditions; the farmer, out of his year's income, is not in a position to pay that rate of interest. It has been said repeatedly in the house; it has been said by members of the cabinet that farmers cannot continue to pay rates of seven, eight or eight to ten per cent. I know insurance companies that have reduced the wages of every one of their employees but that are still insisting on collecting their eight per cent; they are not willing to say to the mortgagor: Conditions have changed so that we realize you are not in a position to pay the eight per cent; we will make dt even seven. Let us admit that the problem is difficult, but the situation is so desperate, and, I may say, in many cases conditions at present are so impossible, parliament would be well advised to deal with the matter, and I think it would be quite within our rights to do so.
With regard to the legal aspect of the question, I think I read the opinion given by all the attorneys general in Canada who replied to a questionnaire sent out last year by the banking committee, and if I remember correctly every one who expressed an opinion said that the dominion government had power to legislate in regard to interest rates even on existing obligations. There is only one way, I suppose, to determine a case like that, and that is to pass the legislation and see what is done about it. I thought that this afternoon when we were discussing matters which were brought up on the other bill. We could pass the legislation and if anybody cared to test its validity in the courts we could soon get a decision as to whether the legislation was ultra vires. I should like again to urge the Prime Minister to take some action to reduce, by legislation, interest rates generally.
To deal with the other question I raised, that is the differential, I really do not think there is any differential fixed in the act, but I speak subject to correction. I am now quoting from the farm loan act of 1627. Section 7, paragraph (e) deals with the rate of interest.

Paragraphs (e) and (f)
are the ones that deal with the problem.

The section reads:
The interest rate on loans under this act shall be such a rate in excess of the interest rate yielded at the time of issue by the last series of farm loan bonds issued by the board as shall be sufficient, in the judgment of the

board, to provide for the expenses of operation and for the necessary reserves for losses, or if no such bonds have been issued, such a rate as in the judgment of the board will be yielded by the farm loan bonds when issued, increased by provision for expenses and reserves as aforesaid.
I take it for granted then that the differential of one and a half per cent is simply a role of the board.
Paragraph (f).

Paragraph (f) reads:
Every farm loan shall be repayable in equal annual or semi-annual instalments of principal and interest at the option of the borrower; and the amount of such instalment or instalments payable in any year shall be a fixed percentage of the amount of the loan, such percentage to be the rate of interest mentioned in the mortgage increased by either one per cent or two per cent of the amount of the loan as the borrower may elect.
I think that provision is simply for the amortization of the principal, so that it would seem that the differential of one and a half per cent is only a rale of the board and not fixed by the act itself. To effect a reduction needs action only by the board, and I think in the present case it might be a matter of government policy to consult the board with a view to having that differential reduced.
I would urge the Prime Minister to take whatever action is necessary to have the interest on loans made by the farm loan board brought down to five per cent. I do not think agriculture can pay a higher rate. We hope in passing these two bills we are taking a really worth while step to deal with this farm debt, and perhaps I should say, farm credit problem. Even at five per cent our farmers will be paying much higher rates than are paid by farmers in many countries. In Denmark the credit societies are borrowing the great bulk of their money at four per cent or less. They did have a large amount outstanding at four and a half per cent, but if I remember correctly, legislation was introduced about two years ago to assist them in converting those four and a half per cent bonds to bonds bearing interest at four per cent, and government action in Denmark has certainly been used to reduce the rate of interest payable on all farm mortgages.

The hon. gentleman will remember that under the provisions of the farm loan act the maximum amount that might 'be loaned was $10,000. In view of the present situation as to values it is believed by officials of the board that the provision limiting the maximum loan to $7,500 would be in the interests of both the borrower and the lender,, in this case the farm loan board.
Just before recess the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) was making a strong appeal for a reduction in the rates of interest.
I need not go over the ground that has been covered so many times this session, but when I say to him that the government has used every means within its power, short of legislative action to which I shall refer presently, to bring about a reduction in interest rates, I think I am stating what is within the know-edge of all. Just what has been accomplished in that regard is also fairly well known, and the price at which money has been loaned to . this dominion recently is some indication of what I have stated. I just put this position to the committee and to my hon. friend. He suggests that this parliament should enact a statute declaring that the interest rates on all outstanding mortgages should be reduced to five per cent; that is, that the rates that now are in excess of five per cent should be reduced to that figure. I say to him that to do so would be hurtful beyond words to the credit of this dominion, and I do not think there is a single member of this committee who does not realize what would be the effect of the arbitrary action of this parliament in reducing the contractual rate to five per cent.
What are we trying to do? On the one hand we are trying to maintain the credit of this country at the highest possible level; on the other hand we are endeavouring to secure all the money we can to meet maturing obligations and also to secure fresh money for needed development. In this very bill there is a provision permitting us to increase the amount of money to be raised by the farm loan board by the sale of bonds. I put this to any hon. member, including the hon. gentleman who has just spoken:	Does he think we
could borrow any money at all outside of Canada-and it would be very difficult in Canada-if by an arbitrary action we declared that all mortgages bearing interest of more than five per cent should have the interest rate reduced to five per cent, depriving those who in good faith have contracted with borrowers of an income, as he suggests, amounting 74726-257J
to several million dollars? Just tell me what the effect would be upon the farmers themselves. The farm loan board would not be able to borrow more money; that is clear. I doubt if the people of Canada would want to loan money to the board. When I suggested to the committee the other day that two enterprises in Canada had borrowed on debentures in Scotland and elsewhere sums of money in one case amounting to $30,000,000 and in the other case to $29,000,000, at the surprisingly high rate of five per cent, as I learned for the first time a few weeks ago, I merely indicated that this was a factor thait had to be considered, because they loaned the money at a higher rate than that at which they borrowed it.
During the discussions that have taken place during the last few months between the government and the representatives of the loan companies I have been greatly taken with the attitude of mind of those representing the lending companies. I recall the words used by one such representative, as follows:
In their own interest, the companies^ do not want the good farmer to abandon his farm or to be sold out; in fact it is the worst thing that can happen to a company at the present time. Therein lies the strongest assurance that can be given that mortgage companies will do. their part in compromise arrangements.
Then he used these words:
As a concrete instance of what is even now being done, I am informed by one loan company that at their weekly board meeting yesterday they dealt with 46 renewals of mortgages in the three prairie provinces. They were all cases where the mortgagor was in arrears for interest, sometimes for a considerable amount. Every renewal was granted, with a reduction in the rate of interest to seven per cent; the arrears of interest were partly waived and the balance capitalized so that the farmer is now given a fresh start with his account in good shape. In addition, further advances were made where necessary for seed or similar necessities.
Then he gives a few extracts from the reports of their inspectors. I mention that to this committee because, in our anxiety to assist, by taking extreme positions sometimes we may harm those whom we desire to assist. We have a condition in this country that has not been brought about in a single day or year, but which has come about after a long series of years. We have made loans to the farmers, amounting to over $700,000,000, as I pointed out when this bill was first brought to the attention of the house. Parliament did not intervene in those days to fix a rate of interest at a rate lower than might be contracted for. To-day the legal rate is five per cent, but parliament has not imposed upon
Farm Loan Act

those who borrow a restriction or prohibition in the exercise of their contractual powers or rights. The result is that a considerable number of mortgages outstanding bear rates of interest in excess of seven per cent, and this was well known to Canada and the Canadian people when it was being done. In the days of buoyant prosperity no one complained about contracting to pay eight per cent; in fact it is well known that sometimes offers of more than eight per cent were made. As a result we are now inheriting a condition. Having inherited that condition we now say that it is beyond our power to emerge from our difficulties unless parliament intervenes and lessens the amount that we must pay to discharge our obligations.
I do not know how many of you read the speech of Mr. John Buchan at the assembly of the Church of Scotland, of which he is high commissioner. He said that at the bottom of all our trouble is fear, which he described as the father of despotism. I made some reference to that on Saturday last. Therein, it seems to me, lies the genesis of much of our trouble. We have made promises. We have executed contracts. We have assumed obligations. With every word that the hon. member for Macleod has said as to the low prices of commodities influencing our ability to pay, we must not forget that the student of history will point out that in days long since past the obligation was to pay ten per cent, twelve per cent, fourteen per cent and fifteen per cent. Without parliamentary intervention or the destruction of contracts it is amazing how the difficulties were met and overcome in the past. The lowering of interest rates; the adjustment of difficulties; the compromise of obligations we have endeavoured to assist in every way within our power, but when you suggest that any government of Canada should arbitrarily say that all mortgages outstanding in this country bearing interest rates of more than five per cent should have those rates reduced to five per cent, and in the same breath suggest to me that we should get more for the farm loan board, I say these are mutually destructive, because if carried out the one will make the other impossible.
Only a few days ago, the day I was absent, I was struck more than I would care to say to this committee with the high reputation that this country enjoys because thus far it has declined to become a party to the destruction of its contractual obligations, and has maintained the position it has taken and met its obligations in the terms of its con-

tracts. I say to my fellow Canadians here to-night that nothing could be more inimical to our credit, nothing could be more destructive to our high reputation and nothing more calculated to menace the very, shall I say, permanent improvement of this country, than that we should listen to what is urged by some in that regard. It is so easy and so popular to raise the cry, " Why don't they cut the interest? Why don't they destroy our contracts?" Mr. Chairman, there is an old saying, a very old one to which I shall refer; I am sure the classic mind of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) will recall the words, " Swift is the descent to hell," and once started upon this course what must be the result? I just leave that with the committee, because I do not purpose again to reargue the matter. It would be so much easier for one to court popular approval in certain quarters by simply saying, "Certainly, we are going to cut these things; we are going to destroy these contracts; we are going to pay no attention to obligations created in the past, but we will just think of the present and of the future." One could get more votes that way, and would please more people. If any hon. member suggests that I am not fully advised of the economic conditions of those who have to pay, and that I have not a clear appreciation of the difficulties they have to overcome and, in many instances, their inability to do so, I can say only this, that he is entirely in error. If any hon. members assume that I have not as much knowledge as they have about the matter, they are wrong. I know about the hardships and the difficulties. But what we did through the bill considered this afternoon was to go to the absolute limit of our constitutional jurisdiction, without destroying our credit. And to-night what we are endeavouring to do is to ensure that there shall be a little fresh capital available to make a start, and that some safeguard shall be provided to prevent the very thing we are trying to do from having the effect of destroying our power to do that which we seek to do.

I have been very much interested in this bill to amend the Canadian Farm Loan Act, which is a companion to the bill we passed this afternoon. As such it must afford relief to a number of farmers throughout our country in order that they may get that for which they have been looking so long. There was a great deal of discussion this afternoon on the bill which now stands for third reading, and I must confess that I am fairly well seized

Farm Loan Act
as to the meaning of that piece of legislation. If I understand it correctly it means, first, that if a farmer finds himself in distressed circumstances he may go to the receiver, and the receiver may say to him, "Let me have the number of your creditors, and their names." Then with that information before him he states, "We will take your case into consideration and, if the situation warrants, we will call the creditors into conference so that we may have a clear understanding of the whole situation." Then, having done that, and there comes a time when all the creditors do not agree, they will say, "We will submit this case to the court of review," upon which occasion the court of review makes the final decision as to whether or not there is a clear case. It seems to me that is absolutely clear, and ought to be a fair arrangement for the farmers. After having gone that far the farmer may find himself unable to meet his obligations, aind he states that he has been unable to meet them; the court of review has then no jurisdiction over him, in which event he goes to the bankruptcy court. I believe that is a correct understanding of the situation. After all this has been done, this bill, which I have described as the companion bill to the one discussed this afternoon, takes effect, and through its operation it is intended if possible to relieve the farmer.
We will suppose that a farmer owes $4,000 and finds that he is unable to pay it. Where will he get that money? My deduction is that it is intended he shall get the money through the farm loan board mentioned in the bill before us. During the last few years I have had some experience with the Canadian Farm Loan Board. 1 do not know what the experience of other hon. member's has been, but in the province of New Brunswick, and in my own constituency particularly, I want to state frankly that we have submitted a large number of cases to the Canadian Farm Loan Board at Ottawa, cases approved by the provincial board and in that respect different from those to which reference was made this afternoon. These cases have gone before the board at Ottawa and time after time have been turned down. I submit that to-day the Canadian Farm Loan Board is simply a collecting agency; it is no longer a lending power. If through the bill before us, which gives additional powers to the Canadian Farm Loan Board to lend on stock and on other securities offered, we get no farther than we have got in the past few years, we will not go very far towards providing money to assist the farmers in their agricultural pursuits. I believe hon. members know that in the past few years the Canadian Farm Loan Board
have not done more than could have been done by a collecting agency.

I suggest that the hon. member is quite out of order; in fact, all this discussion in my view has been out of order. We are now discussing section 5, which has nothing to do with the general principle of the bill. With all due deference to the hon. member I suggest he should confine himself to the subject under discussion.
I presumed that section 5 of the bill was wide enough to permit my going into the whole matter.
Section 5 of the bill limits the amount of money the board may lend. I shall read it.

I beg your pardon; I can read it. That is exactly the point with which I was dealing. I was referring to the amount of money to be lent, and I am very sorry that I did not impress 3rou, Mr. Chairman, with that fact. So far as this bill is concerned it is entirely of the same pattern as the one we passed this afternoon, and the question of lending money is absolutely relevant, I submit. If the farmers cannot get loans from the farm loan board to relieve them in their present distress, they cannot get very far.
If I understood the Prime Minister aright, he said this afternoon he was not sure that borrowers under the Canadian Farm Loan Act and under the Soldier Settlement Act could obtain money under this act. Is that correct?

was my understanding at least of the Prime Minister's remarks. If we are going to relieve the farmers we must see that they get a lower rate of interest. If there is one thing that is burdening the farmers more than another it is the high rate of interest.
Again let me draw the attention of the committee to the fact that this section has nothing to do with interest. The hon. gentleman is absolutely out of order.

I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, if I have digressed from the section before us but I had a few observations to make in connection with the lending of money to farmers, and if this is not the right time I shall reserve my remarks until a subsequent section.

I was interested in the
very able case which the Prime Minister made with regard to keeping up the credit of Canada. But there are two distinct sides to that subject, one of which I do not think he stressed enough. If Canada is suffering at all with regard to credit it is because fifty per cent of her people who are on the land are facing a serious financial crisis, and I think it is just as necessary to pay attention to the huge losses that have been incurred by those who have lost fifty to sixty per cent of their commodity wealth as to the possible losses of the financial wealth of other people,
I should like to say a word or two in support of the remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat with regard to the administration of the loans of the Canadian Farm Loan Board. I have had an enormous correspondence in regard to this matter in the last two years, and I regret to say that I have never had a letter which has been complimentary to the administration of these loans.
I want to congratulate the government on Bill 92, which may prove to be one of the best pieces of legislation which has been passed by this house to help the farmer to get back on his feet. But if the bill now before us is intended to be complementary to Bill 92, very serious changes will have to be made in the administration of the farm
(Mr. B. F. Smith.]
loan act. Not only are the officials of the board collectors at the present time, but they are collectors in the roughest sense of the term. I hold in my hand a letter I received this morning-

I would call the attention of the hon. gentleman to a ruling I made a few moments ago.
I must rule the hon. gentleman out of order.

I do not want to go
against your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but the type of collection in the last few years has been one of the worst, and it has been done at a time when the farmer is in a very serious financial condition through no fault of his own. It has been nothing less than brutal, to say the least.

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, this bill received its second reading with practically no discussion, and in such cases it is usual to allow a certain amount of discussion on the principle of the bill when we are in committee. That is the common practice in this house, and it is very unusual for the chairman to insist upon every member of the Committee keeping strictly to. the clause under discussion when there has been no debate on the principle on second reading. I think it will facilitate the work of the committee and of the house to allow that much discussion. Certainly the question of interest is involved in the question of the amount of money the board may lend, and that is one of the questions dealt with in this section.

I think the hon. gentleman is well enough acquainted with the rules of the house. All I have to do is to quote subsection 2 of rule 58 which reads:
Speeches in committee of the whole house must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
The hon. gentleman is sufficiently acquainted with the rules to know that a general discussion is not in order when the committee is discussing a section of a bill, and I submit that hon. gentlemen would assist the business of the house by complying with the rules.

Speaking to the point of order, Mr. Chairman, a thing I very rarely do, I submit that when the committee is dealing with a clause which applies specifically to the conditions under which loans may be made and to the limitations upon those loans, is the very time to discuss all the conditions surrounding the loan-the way the loans are made and how they are collected. To my mind there could be no clause on which a discus-

Farm Loan Act
sion of interest rates and of the general policy in respect to the issue of loans would be more relevant than on the one now before us, which deals with the power of the board to make loans, the limitations placed by the board upon such loans, and generally the conditions under which loans are made. It seems to me, therefore, 'Mr. Chairman, that we are very much in order in discussing this particular phase at this time.
I do not want to limit the discussion on a question of this kind, and if the committee desires to permit hon. members to ramble on as they have, it is all right with me.

I take it I wouild be in order if I spoke in connection with section 5. This reads:
Loans shall be made only on the security of first mortgages on farm lands ...
And so on. My point is that while this section says that they shall be made, the Canadian Farm Loan Board has refused to make any loans within the district which I represent. No matter what the security is, no matter what the buildings are, no matter what the character of the individual may be, no matter what his record may be with regard to that which he has produced, the Canadian Farm Loan Board has thought it unwise to lend within that district. Generally speaking, these loans run over a number of years. In the years 1925, 1926, 1927 and 1928 this district produced perhaps the best crops in Manitoba. For a period of three or four years since that time there have been no crops in the western section of that area. The regular mortgage companies which hold mortgages within this area have refused to continue to lend. At a time when we expected we should get some assistance from the Canadian Farm Loan Board, they have adopted precisely the same attitude and have refused to lend. It seems to me that this board from the point of view of policy, from the point of view of the Canadian people and from the point of view of good business has not adopted the right attitude by saying that because there have been no crops for two or three years they will not advance any money. Particularly is that so when no consideration is given to the past record of the farmer and particularly so because these mortgages, generally speaking, run for a period of twenty years. I take it that this was not the purpose of the setting up of the Canadian Farm Loan Board. I readily realize that the government has no control over the policies of the farm loan board, as it is an independent body set up for that purpose. My criticism is with
regard to the judgment of the farm loan board and its adoption of that attitude. Why is it that a farmer who produced twenty-five or thirty bushels to the acre in 1928, who has good buildings, who has a good record as a farmer, whose lands, machinery, cattle and horses are unencumbered, should not be permitted to get a loan? He may be a good man; he may have good possibilities, but this farm loan board has completely blocked out that area and said that no loans shall be made irrespective of the individual, his security or his possibilities. In my opinion that was not the purpose for which the Canadian Farm Loan Board was set up. If an area produced good crops from 1925 to 1928, it is quite reasonable to suppose that it will produce good crops from 1935 to 1938. The farm loan board was willing to make loans in this area up to 1928 at a time when there were poor crops in other areas, but when those other areas are having fair crops and this area is having none, they refuse to make loans. It seems to me that the policy of the board is open to very severe criticism in connection with the way they have handled this situation. I say it is not good business and it is not the purpose for which the board was set up. In my opinion the purposes for which this board was set up are not being carried out by the present management.

Paragraph (a) of section 7 of the present act states that:

mortgages taken as security for farm loans and remedies thereunder shall be in all respects subject to the law of the province in which the farm land mortgaged is situated.
Under section 5 of the bill paragraph (a) of section 7 of the act is being repealed, and as I understand the substituted paragraph, it will mean that any loans now taken out will not be subject to the law of the particular province in which the land is situated. I understand that private companies making loans come under the laws of the province in which the loans are made, and I should like to know why the farm loan board should not be placed in the same category.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Lucas) must be ill advised as there is no change in the law. Section 7 is being amended and in lieu of the existing paragraph (a) a mew paragraph is being substituted. This paragraph does not deal with the matter to which the hon. member has referred, it merely limits the amount to $7,500. It is not necessary to provide that mortgages taken as security on a farm shall be in all respects subject to the law of the province in which the farm land mortgaged is
Farm Loan Act

situated, because that is a matter implied; it is a matter of law. It was put in the original act, but it was really unnecessary.
Does the Prime Minister say that there is no change?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Except as to the amount.

I notice the last sentence in the explanatory note reads:
This provision, in view of the extension of loaning operations provided in Part II of this bill, is not included in the amended subsection.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Surely, but it does not change that.

I have no criticism to make of the general purpose of this bill and the other bill providing for the possibility of a farmer making a composition to his creditors. If the intentions can be carried out, no doubt the results will be good. However, I am just a little doubtful as to whether it will be possible for farmers to make any great use of either of these bills. This section provides that loans shall be made only on the security of first mortgages on farm lands up to fifty per cent of the boards appraised value of such land and twenty per cent of the permanent insured improvements thereon. If a farmer takes action under the other bill and has his mortgage reduced to a given amount, I think it will be found in many cases that that amount will be more than the amount at which any appraiser would value the lands under present day conditions. Land is not productive to-day because it will not pay the cost of working it. Many farmers have mortgages of from $5,000 to $6,000. Suppose a farmer makes a composition and his mortgage is reduced from $6,000 to $4,000; I believe that those in charge of the operations of the farm loan board will find that $4,000 is too large an amount and will only lend the farmer about $2,000. That will leave the farmer in a position where it will be impossible to take advantage of either of these bills. As I say, I have no criticism to make of the government for their endeavour to solve this problem; I am fully aware of the difficulties which confront them, but I cannot help thinking that the situation which I have depicted is one that is very likely to happen: Some of the machine companies a year ago made a very good offer to their debtors; they offered to take $100 in payment of $112 of debt. That was very good for those who could take advantage of it; but if a man did not have $100-and it was not much easier to get $100 than $112-the offer was not of much use to him. I am just afraid that in many instances PVtr. Bennett.]
some such situation will develop in the actual working out of these two measures we have been considering, good though they may be in intention.

Would
it not be possible to have some appeal from the final decision of the Canadian Farm Loan Board? I realize that there will be a great responsibility on the government of the country, but on the other hand I do submit that under the circumstances, in view of the fact that provision is made for appeal from the marketing board as well as in all other acts that we have passed, there ought to be an appeal from the decision of the Canadian Farm Loan Board.

I was somewhat relieved when the Prime Minister said that there was no change in that feature of the act which brought loans made by the farm loan board under provincial protective legislation such as the debt adjustment and moratorium acts. Is the Prime Minister quite certain? If he is, then the explanatory paragraph is entirely misleading. Section 5 states that paragraph (a) of section 7 is repealed "and the following is substituted therefor," and that substitution deals with the amount of loan which may be made upon first class mortgages. The explanatory paragraph reads:
The present paragraph (a) of section 7 fixes the maximum loan on first mortgage security at ten thousand dollars. This amendment reduces the amount of the maximum loan to seventy-five hundred dollars to conform with the maximum of the advances on first and second mortgage security fixed by section 9 of this bill.
The present paragraph (a) further provides that "mortgages taken as security for farm loans and remedies thereunder shall be in all respects subject to the law of the province in which the farm land mortgaged is situate." In virtue thereof, the board has been subject, in the handling of its loans, to the provisions of all provincial debt adjustment and moratorium legislation. This provision, in view of the extension of loaning operations provided in Part II of this bill, is not included in the amended subsection.
So that it would appear to be deleted from this part of the act. But the Prime Minister states that in spite of that deletion, as a matter of common law it will fall under the protective legislation in the provinces.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think I should make
it somewhat clearer than that. The law of the province as to the form of mortgage and all rights and remedies of the mortgagee governs, of course. The debt adjustment act, as a matter of legal opinion, has no reference to it; but in view of the language used in

Farm Loan Act
the section, an argument has been built up that the parliament of Canada conferred jurisdiction upon them. That was never intended to be so, because, to be perfectly frank with the hon. gentleman, it is believed by many of those even responsible for debt adjustment acts that they are ultra vires of provincial legislatures in matters of this kind; hence it is they have been very anxious that some such act as that which was passed this afternoon should have been on our statute books. For it is quite obvious that it is a form of bankruptcy that is being carried on under the guise of provincial legislation, and this section as amended leaves it not open to controversy on the ground set up, namely, that the federal power made the mortgages subject in all respects to the law of the province; and they said that one of the respects was the debt adjustment act, which in our opinion is not an argument based on sound law. I should have made that more lengthy explanation but I thought, from the way the hon. member for Camrose spoke, that that was what he had in mind. I am glad to have had occasion to make this more extended explanation.

I assume then that the only part of this explanatory paragraph which is misleading is that which states that by virtue of the second part of the original subsection (a) the loans made by the farm loan board did come within the purview and under the authority of provincial protective legislation such as the debt adjustment and moratorium acts.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Rather than have long, complicated lawsuits the matter is dealt with in this rather than in the other way.

The great agricultural province of Saskatchewan has its fair share of farmers in debt and unable to carry on, and who do not come within the purview of this federal farm loan act. We have provincial legislation whereby farmers have been able to get loans up to, I believe, a maximum of $9,000,000 or $10,000,000, but in recent years the provincial government has been unable to get money to make further loans. Here we are extending the scope of this legislation from $15,000,000 up to $40,000,000. Is there not some way whereby, if money cannot be advanced directly from the federal farm loan board to finance individual farmers in Saskatchewan, the provincial farm loan scheme of Saskatchewan can be financed from this, so that farmers in that province may at least be on an equal footing with the farmers in other provinces.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman knows perhaps that there are those who used to assert that they were much better off under their act than they would be under this. I do not know just what steps might be taken to meet that situation. When the bill has been finished in committee and stands for third reading I will go over it again and if we can think out any plan by which what has been suggested can be done we shall see that in another place a clause is added to the bill. This question has been giving us a considerable amount of thought but it is not as easy as it appears to arrive at a solution. The farm loan board does not operate in Saskatchewan and we cannot select some other instrumentality that will make advances and over which we ourselves would have control.
Farm Loan Act

speechtext: Ontario does not.

My

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Substantially that is right as the law now stands. The amortization fund of two per cent to which an hon. member referred this afternoon is two per cent on account of the principal; it has nothing to do with the interest. I think this afternoon I directed the attention of the committee to the matter. It will be recalled that the appraised value is the value for productive purposes and the interest rate was to be, as the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) read this afternoon under paragraph (e) of section 7, a rate that would return the interest on the money borrowed and provide for the expenses of operation and the necessary reserves for losses, or, if no bonds were issued, such a rate as in the judgment of the board would be yielded by the farm loan bonds when issued, increased by provision for expenses and reserves. At the present time the board has fixed one and a half per cent in addition to the going rate. If therefore, three and a half per cent money was secured, that money would be lent at a maximum of five per cent.

It has been moved by the Prime Minister that the word "forty" be inserted before the word "million" in line eleven, section 8 of the bill and that in the fifteenth line the words "thirty million" be inserted before the word "dollars."

On section 9-Further loan may be made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have an amendment to move to this clause. If the committee will be good enough to look at it they will observe that the first mortgage loan is limited in practice to a maximum of less than fifty per cent

of the appraised value of the land plus twenty per cent of the value of the buildings, and with the further advance it will be seen that the total advance would be approximately sixty per cent. I am therefore changing the figures so that subclause 2 of clause 9 will read:
The aggregate of loans made to any one borrower under the provisions of this act and of the Canadian Farm Loan Act shall not exceed two-thirds of the appraised value of the land and buildings in respect of "which security is taken and' shall not exceed at any one time the sum of $7,500. The amount advanced under this section shall not exceed one-half the amount advanced on the security of the first mortgage.
It will be observed that the clause read "one-third." That would have brought about a condition that we are trying to avoid rather than create. The amendment may be made in one of two ways, either substitute the new subclause or change the wording. The amendment will be to strike out the word "one-third" in the thirty-fourth line of clause 9 and substitute therefor the word "one-half".

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

Just in this connection, in comparing the clause we aire just passing with clause 3 of the first part of the bill, I am afraid there might be some contradiction, not in law but in practice. Under clajuse 3 of the first part of the bill we provide that the board may accept and hold additional collateral security for loans as the board may deem proper. In answer to a question that was asked whether the farmer might be forced to offer this additional security, the Prime Minister said: no, as a matter of his own choice. But from such experience as we have had I am not certain that it will be because, although strictly speaking it may be a matter of his own choice, if a farmer fails into arrears of payment the board might well suggest this would be carried forward and no action would be taken if the additional collateral were given. That having been done-and I am afraid it may be done in a good many cases unless there is a little more leniency shown in administration-farmers who have loans from the board at present would be debarred from securing those additional loans on live stock and personal property which are contemplated in the latter part of the measure. Of course that would not apply to new loans made because they would be made definitely under present conditions, but it might readily apply to a large part of the eight or nine millions now outstanding if the board exercises its power in that way.

Farm Loan Act

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I can give no assurance
how the board will exercise its powers, but the words in clause 3 must be read with the words that follow: "May deem proper."
And "deem proper" means proper under the terms of this legislation, that is as to the advances the board makes. The limitations imposed in clause 9 of course prevail and it will be observed that the interest rate on this loan will be only one per cent more and not one and one-half, than is paid for the money; that is because of the character of the loan the clause so provides.

I was reading paragraph (g) which is the second paragraph in clause 3 and that covered the very point I had in mind. It is to enable the board to-
Make such composition, extension of time or scheme of arrangement with any borrower on his loan as the board deems advisable.
It would simply put it into the power of the board in case of any farmer who was unable to meet his obligations promptly _ to insist on receiving this additional security. The additional security being covered by an existing loan, the farmer would be precluded from receiving the additional loan contemplated in the second part of the bill. That was the point I had in mind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I intend to move an
amendment to this clause. The other day I promised that we would look it over a little more carefully. It will be observed that subsection 1 provides for loans to the mortgagee on the security of the assignment of the first mortgage in any province in which the board is empowered to make loans. Then instead of subsection 2 we propose the following :
Whenever a proposal for a composition, extension or scheme of arrangement made under The Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act has been duly approved, the mortgagee shall be eligible for a loan which shall be disbursed to the farmer for such purpose in connection
with the proper operation of the farm lands covered by the first mortgage and in such instalments as may be agreed to by the board.
That is to ensure that the money thus advanced goes for' the purposes for which the new loan is made. It is not intended to designate them here; they are such as may be agreed upon by the farmer and the board. Then there is an amendment to be inserted as subsection 8 immediately after subsection 7, as follows:
The provisions of section five of the Canadian Farm Loan Act for the issue of capital stock and subscriptions therefor shall not apply with respect to loans made under this section.
This amendment is proposed for reasons that were given the other day by one of the hon. members of this committee. Then we further propose the insertion of the following as subsection 9:
The governor in council may make advances to the board out of any unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund for the purposes of this section and the board shall, for such purposes, be deemed to be the agent of the crown and any securities taken by the board shall be so taken on behalf of the crown.
I know my hon. friends opposite have strong views with regard to this procedure, but for reasons which I mentioned the other day it seems to me that in the first instance we cannot do better than this. After this has been in operation during the next fiscal year we will be able to predict what is to be done with some degree of certainty. It will be recalled that we have a control over all the moneys because they are raised under a preceding section and are dealt with in a report made by the farm loan board. It is also the intention to renumber the present subsection 8 as subsection 10.

How are the moneys provided in the original act?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

The hon. gentleman will remember that the board had power to issue and sell bonds known as Canadian farm loan bonds; to make long term loans; to hold real estate, and so on. We were to subscribe a *certain amount of the capital, not to exceed [Mr. Neill.)
$5,000,000, which was the first capital the company had. After that they sold their bonds' entirely to the Minister of Finance; there have been no public issues so far. The moneys have been borrowed by the country and advanced to the board. Five per cent was to be subscribed by the province and five per cent by the borrower; the rate of interest was to be approximately five per cent, and the bonds were to be for thirty-five years. There is nothing further than that.

I thought the amendment provided for funds under Part II of this act, regarding supplementary advances, being paid out of the unappropriated portion of the consolidated revenue fund, and I was wondering why these funds were not provided as in the original act, namely through the sale of bonds.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

That is how it is hoped
the money will be secured later. You see, it is limited to one-quarter the amount of the mortgage, and the officials thought that the only method by which they would be certain of being able to have the money, in the event of difficulties such as I have indicated, would be to make it a charge against the consolidated revenue fund. It would be a little difficult to issue bonds for the purpose of securing money to be advanced on the equivalent of chattel mortgages. And so, in order not to leave that impression too strongly, that we have engaged in that business, we make it a charge against the consolidated revenue fund, in the first instance, but it is for only a year, and limited to one-quarter the amount of the mortgage. I believe it is one-quarter, at any rate.

The right hon. gentleman knows what I am referring to. He knows that the right hon. leader of the opposition has always felt that these funds should be provided by vote, and that moneys needed for purposes of this kind should come from moneys appropriated by parliament for the purpose, not out of the unappropriated portion of the consolidated revenue fund. I was wondering if the Prime Minister had considered that point, and if it would be possible to have that provision in here, because we can estimate somewhere near the amount of money which would be required.

Last year I drew the minister's attention to the fact that people who live in cities such as Vancouver or New Westminster are able to obtain the services of radio interference inspectors, and I urged that the same service should be given to people living in the rural parts. This item is for the celebration of the four hundredth anniversary of the landing of Jacques Cartier, and I notice that $100,000 is to be distributed in Gaspe, Three Rivers, Ottawa and Niagara. I do not wish to oppose the granting of this amount but I would call attention to the fact that the place of Jacques Cartier's first landing, in what is now known as the Dominion of Canada, was not on the Gaspe coast but at the entrance to Bathurst harbour. According to the description given in history of his peregrinations in the straits of Northumberland and the bay of Chaleur, he landed first on what is now Canadian soil at the entrance to Bathurst harbour, now known as Caron Point. I do not think the government should have left Bathurst out entirely in the distribution of this amount. I want it to become a matter of general history that the fact is as I have stated.

I may state now that the extreme language of the oath of allegiance which is preserved to this day was first adopted by the legislature of IJjpper Canada at a time when the grandfather of the right hon. gentleman, having been a member, had been expelled. Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 10.20 p.m.
Tuesday, June 19, 1934
